Belgian road accidents 2017-2024

Which road user bears the greatest accident burden?

289,532 accidents, compared across road-user groups. An accident counts once for every group it involves (road user 1 or 2), so one accident can count for two groups. These are counts, not rates per amount of traffic.

1a

Who is involved

Blue = a named road-user group. Gray = not a specific group (Unknown, Other road user).

Key findings

Fixed text for all years 2017-2024; it does not change with the filters.

  • Passenger cars (70.2% of all accidents) and bicycles (24.8%) are involved most often. Pedestrians follow at 10.3%, vans 8.1%, mopeds 8.0%, motorcycles 6.8%, trucks 4.4%, buses 1.4%.
  • "Unknown" is 10.7%: for about one accident in ten the road user is not recorded.
  • Shares add up to more than 100% because one accident can involve two groups (136,144 accidents involve two different groups).

Read with care: these are raw counts. A group that is common on the road appears often for that reason alone; severity and traffic volume are not part of this graph.

1b

Annual change

Key findings

Fixed text for all years 2017-2024; it does not change with the filters.

  • Almost every group drops in 2020 (bicycles only -5.5%; buses -37.7% and pedestrians -30.4% most) and rebounds in 2021-2022.
  • By 2024 (2017 = 100): bicycles 115, mopeds 105, vans and buses 97, pedestrians 86, motorcycles 83, passenger cars 82, trucks 73.
  • Post vs pre (average per year 2022-2024 against 2017-2019): trucks -17.2%, motorcycles -12.9%, cars -12.2%, pedestrians -10.4%, buses -6.4%, vans +1.5%, mopeds +7.3%, bicycles +14.6%.
  • "Unknown" more than doubles (+113% from 2017 to 2024). Part of the decline of the named groups may be recording shifting into "Unknown"; the data cannot show that.

Read with care: "Covid-19" is my own label for the periods. These are accident counts, not rates, so fewer accidents could also mean less traffic.

1c

Months and seasons

Months (heatmap)

Colour = seasonal index (blue below an average month, red above; 100 = average). Numbers = the measure chosen above. The index is not corrected for month length: February has 28 or 29 days; use "Per day" to correct for that.

Seasons (grouped bars)

The number marks each group's highest season. Winter, spring, summer and autumn have 90-92 days, so an even share of 25% is approximate.

Key findings

Fixed text for all years 2017-2024; it does not change with the filters.

  • Motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds peak in the warm months and nearly vanish in winter: motorcycles have 13.0% of their accidents in winter and 32.6% in summer.
  • Pedestrians are the reverse: highest share in winter (28.0%), lowest in summer (21.3%), with a peak in December (index 123).
  • Passenger cars, vans and trucks are fairly even, with a mild autumn peak (about 27%).
  • Per day, January is the quietest month for all accidents (84.8 a day), not February (91.2); February's low index is partly its length.
  • In 2020-2021 the spring share is lower for every group (all accidents 20.6% against 25.1% before); from 2022 the pattern looks like before again. The data states no cause.

Read with care: shares and indexes describe WHEN a group's accidents happen, not how many there are, and not rates per amount of traffic. The seasonal hypotheses (riding in good weather, darker months for pedestrians) are not tested.

2

Severity

Who experiences the most severe outcomes? Fixed results from my analysis scripts, not recalculated here: the years filter on the left does not apply to sections 2 to 5. The severity class belongs to the WHOLE accident, not to one road user: a car-pedestrian accident counts for both groups.

Period

Share of each group's accidents that are fatal, seriously injured or slightly injured

Dot = share, line = 95% interval, gray line = all accidents. Pre, during and post Covid-19 are my own period names; the data states no cause.

Severity distribution per group

Key findings

Fixed text for all years 2017-2024; it does not change with the controls.

  • Accidents involving trucks and motorcycles are the most severe: fatal plus serious makes up 17.3% (trucks) and 18.9% (motorcycles) of their accidents, against 9.9% for all accidents.
  • The fatal share is 5.1% for trucks (3.6 times the 1.4% of all accidents), 2.8% for motorcycles and 2.0% for pedestrians. It is lowest for mopeds (0.6%), bicycles (0.9%) and passenger cars (1.3%).
  • Bicycle accidents are less often fatal but more often seriously injured (10.0% against 8.4% overall); motorcycles have the highest serious share (16.2%).
  • The fatal share of all accidents falls from 1.54% (2017-2019) to 1.47% (2020-2021) and 1.29% (2022-2024).

Read with care: these are the severity of the accidents a group is part of, not the harm to that group's own members. A truck accident may be fatal mostly for the other party. They are shares given that an accident happened, not the risk of having one. Intervals assume independent accidents, which is slightly optimistic because one accident can count for two groups.

Geography

Where are vulnerable road users most exposed? Fixed results (the years filter does not apply). Municipality outlines: Statbel statistical sectors 2023, CC BY 4.0 (outlines joined and simplified).

3a. Accidents involving cyclists, by municipality, 2017-2024

Map

Key findings

Fixed text for all years 2017-2024; it does not change with the controls.

  • 71,881 accidents involve cyclists, in 577 of the 581 municipalities; cyclists are in 24.8% of all accidents.
  • By count: Antwerpen 7,405 (37% of its accidents), Gent 4,229 (42%), Brussel 2,478 (25%), Leuven 1,773 (54%), Brugge 1,598 (37%).
  • By share (municipalities with 100+ accidents): Haacht 56.2%, Mortsel 54.4%, Leuven 54.3%, Hove 50.4%, Keerbergen 49.0%.
  • Cyclist share by region: Flanders 33.5%, Brussels 21.8%, Wallonia 7.0%. Wherever cyclists make up more than a third of the accidents, the municipality is in Flanders.

Read with care: counts favour big cities and the data has no population or cycling-traffic figures, so these are not rates per inhabitant or per cyclist.

3b / 3c. Hotspots: pedestrians, motorcycles and mopeds (500 m squares)

Group
Years

Key findings

Fixed text for all years 2017-2024; it does not change with the controls.

  • Pedestrians: 17 of the top 20 squares are in the Brussels area, 2 in Antwerp and 1 in Liège; the busiest square (Antwerp) has 82 accidents, only 0.31% of all located pedestrian accidents.
  • Motorcycles: all 20 busiest squares are in the Brussels area (busiest: 41 accidents).
  • Mopeds: 12 of the top 20 squares are in Antwerp, 4 in Gent, 2 in Brussels, 1 in Charleroi and 1 in Knokke-Heist (busiest: 45 accidents).
  • About two thirds of the hotspot squares come back in 2022-2024 (12, 16 and 12 of 20 for pedestrians, motorcycles and mopeds).

Read with care: hotspots are where accidents are COUNTED, which is mostly where many people and vehicles are; there are no traffic or population figures. 10-13% of accidents have no coordinates (3-5% in 2022-2024), more in Wallonia, so Walloon hotspots may be understated. Different square sizes would give different ranks.

    Regions and concentration

    Regional differences in severity, concentration against severity, and the regional gap at the same density. Fixed results (the years filter does not apply). The severity class belongs to the whole accident; concentration is where accidents are counted, not traffic.

    4a. Regional severity

    Fatal and serious share per region and province, all accidents. Brussels has no province.

    Province map

    By road-user group

    Within each road type

    Hollow dots = fewer than 100 accidents; they can run off the panel. Mwy = motorway, Reg = regional road, Mun = municipal road.

    Key findings

    Fixed text for all years 2017-2024; it does not change with the controls.

    • Fatal share: Wallonia 2.26% (1.6 times Belgium), Flanders 1.23%, Brussels 0.42%. Serious-injury share goes the other way: Flanders 9.67%, Wallonia 7.16%, Brussels 4.45%.
    • By province, the fatal share is highest in Luxembourg (3.37%), Namur (2.95%) and Hainaut (2.17%) and lowest in Antwerp (1.04%) and Brussels (0.42%); the serious share is highest in West Flanders (11.5%).
    • The order Brussels < Flanders < Wallonia in fatal share holds for cyclists, pedestrians, motorcycles and mopeds.
    • Wallonia has the higher fatal share on every road type: motorways 4.01% against 2.39% in Flanders, regional roads 2.54% against 1.22%, municipal roads 1.52% against 1.02%.

    Read with care: Flanders has more serious but fewer fatal accidents than Wallonia. That could be real or come from how the classes are recorded; I have not tested it. Matching road type controls for road type only.

    4b. Concentration against severity

    By the number of accidents in the 500 m square (accidents with coordinates, two periods); hollow dots = fewer than 100 accidents.

    By municipality density

    Five equal-sized classes of accidents per km2 per year (of that group).

    One dot per municipality

    rho = Spearman rank correlation between density and severity share. Only municipalities with at least 100 accidents (for a group: at least 30 of its accidents).

    Key findings

    Fixed text for all years 2017-2024; it does not change with the controls.

    • The busier the square, the less severe the accidents: for all accidents the fatal share falls from 3.00% in squares with one accident to 0.37% in squares with 100 or more; the serious share from 12.5% to 5.1%.
    • The same direction holds for cyclists (fatal 1.93% to 0.17%), pedestrians (4.29% to 0.70%), motorcycles and mopeds, and in 2022-2024 as well.
    • By municipality: the fatal share falls from 3.66% in the least dense fifth to 0.80% in the densest; Spearman rho is -0.66 for all accidents, -0.52 for motorcycles, -0.36 for pedestrians, -0.22 for cyclists and -0.15 for mopeds.
    • The accident hotspots are therefore not the deadliest places: an isolated pedestrian accident is fatal in 4.3% of cases, one in a busy square in under 1%.

    Read with care: this is an association, not a cause. Dense places have lower speeds, other roads and more minor accidents, and density is accidents per km2, not per vehicle.

    4c. Regions within the same density

    Is the Wallonia-Flanders gap still there when municipalities of the same accident density (and road type) are compared? Regions within the same density class, all accidents:

    Per road-user group

    Each group has its own density classes.

    Within the same density class AND road type, all accidents

    How much of the Wallonia-Flanders gap remains

    Above 1 = Wallonia higher. Standardised ratio: Wallonia's share if it had Flanders' mix of strata. Odds ratio: logistic regression with bootstrap intervals (1,000 repetitions).

    Key findings

    Fixed text for all years 2017-2024; it does not change with the controls.

    • At the same accident density Wallonia's fatal share stays 36-48% higher than Flanders' in every density class (ratio 1.48, 1.36, 1.36, 1.37 and 1.44); overall the ratio is 1.84.
    • Adjusted odds ratio Wallonia vs Flanders, fatal: 1.86 (region only), 1.39 (same density class), 1.35 (also same road type; 95% interval 1.25-1.44). Density and road type explain more than half of the excess; roughly 40% of it remains.
    • The serious-injury gap goes the other way and widens when matched: odds ratio 0.72 crude and 0.60 at the same density and road type.
    • By group (fatal, density + road type): mopeds 1.70 (gap remains), pedestrians 1.23 and motorcycles 1.21 (borderline), cyclists 0.69 (no gap; the standardised ratio's interval includes 1, so I treat it as "no clear gap").

    Read with care: density and road type are the only things matched; speed limits, vehicle mix, enforcement, emergency response and how classes are recorded are not. Brussels is only in the densest class.

    Statistical models

    Logistic models of accident severity (Severe = fatal, fatally injured or seriously injured), with standard errors clustered by municipality. Fixed study results; the filters on the left do not apply. To explore your own selection (years, region, road and light conditions, group comparisons, live models and exports) run the interactive Streamlit tool: code and instructions on GitHub.

    The five models

    One model at a time

    Model
    Show

    The chosen model only. Odds ratios: filled dot = significant at 5%.

    Comparing the five models

    Show

    Key findings

    Fixed text for all years 2017-2024; it does not change with the controls.

    • Baseline model (289,532 accidents, 28,532 severe): the odds of a severe accident are 3.44 times higher with a motorcycle involved and 3.32 times higher with a pedestrian (against a car-only accident), 2.94 with a truck and 1.77 with a bicycle.
    • Night without public lighting raises the odds (1.78 in the baseline; 2.04 for pedestrians and 2.01 for motorcyclists). Brussels has much lower odds than Flanders in every model (0.29 to 0.41), Wallonia somewhat lower (0.74 to 0.81).
    • In the group models a truck as counterpart is the strongest risk factor (odds 5.22 for pedestrians, 4.26 for cyclists, 2.63 for mopeds, 2.26 for motorcyclists, against a passenger car).
    • Accidents in the same municipality are correlated (ICC 0.016 in the baseline); the cluster-robust standard errors are on average 11% larger in the baseline and up to 3.8 times larger for region-level terms.
    • The road users in one accident do not simply add up: 22 pairs were tested jointly (p < 10-180). Bicycle + pedestrian is far less severe than the two effects added (0.33), car + motorcycle more severe (1.48); the order of road user 1 and 2 also matters (p = 2 x 10-9), but their meaning is undocumented.
    • Predicted probability in a daytime urban situation in 2024: car-only accident 5.1%, bicycle against a car 8.6%, pedestrian 15.0%, motorcycle 15.5%.

    Read with care: these are associations, not causes; speed, traffic, vehicle type and helmet use are not in the data. The class belongs to the whole accident. AUC is in-sample. "With a pedestrian" (collision type) is 99% the same as the pedestrian road-user term and is left out of the models; without collision type the pedestrian odds ratio is 2.54 instead of 3.32.

    About and caveats

    • Data: Belgian road-accident open data 2017-2024 (289,532 accidents), translated to English. One row = one accident (the data has no ID to prove it).
    • Counting: an accident counts for a road-user group if that group is road user 1 or road user 2, once per accident. "Single road user" is not a road user.
    • Unknown (about 10% of accidents, growing over the years) and Other road user are separate lines and hidden by default.
    • Periods: pre (2017-2019), during (2020-2021) and post (2022-2024) "Covid-19" are my own definition; the data states no cause.
    • Counts, not rates: traffic volume is not in the data, so more accidents does not mean more risk per kilometre.
    • Seasons: meteorological, whole months only (the data has no day). December, January and February of the same calendar year are grouped.
    • Open questions: why empty coordinates jump in Brussels in 2024; the difference between accident classes "with fatalities" and "fatally injured".
    • Not done: urban vs rural. The data has only "built-up area", no official urban/rural classification (decision #55).
    Decisions behind this dashboard: decision log, entries #60-#69, #109-#114 and #132-#145. Code and data: GitHub.
